title: Chapter 2: History of Tripura — Ancient and Medieval Period

blocks.content: 2.1 Ancient History — Mythological and Early Origins

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Unakoti represents the grandest archaeological site in Tripura's history.
The Manikya Dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Tripura from 1280 to 1949 CE.
The Rajmala serves as the official royal chronicle of Tripura.
Bir Chandra Manikya is known as 'The Great Moderniser' for his rule between 1862 and 1896.

blocks.content: Tripura's name has several explanations. The most popular one is that it derives from 'Tripura Sundari' — one of the ten Mahavidyas (manifestations of Goddess Durga/Shakti), whose temple at Udaipur is one of the 51 Shakti Peethas of India. Another explanation is that it comes from 'Twipra' — the name of an ancient tribe who called themselves Twipra (meaning 'by the water' — 'twi' = water, 'pra' = near). The region finds mention in the epics (Mahabharata) and in the writings of Greek geographer Ptolemy as 'Tippera.'

items: Mahabharata mentions: The region is identified with 'Tripura' in the epic; the Pandavas are said to have passed through the region
Puranic references: The Ashta Bhuja (eight-armed) idol at Tripura Sundari temple is said to be self-manifested (Swayambhu)
Ptolemy's Geography (2nd century CE): Mentions 'Tippera' in his geographical account of the Indian subcontinent
The Twipra people are believed to be among the earliest inhabitants, predating all other tribes

Rock carvings at Unakoti (North Tripura): Date approximately to the 7th–9th century CE; over 1 lakh (100,000) rock-cut images of Shiva and other deities — one of the most extraordinary archaeological sites in northeast India
Pilak (South Tripura): Archaeological site with Buddhist and Hindu sculptures dating to 8th–12th century CE; terracotta figurines, stone sculptures discovered

blocks.content: Unakoti, literally meaning 'one less than a crore' (i.e., 9,999,999), is a Shaivite pilgrimage site and archaeological treasure in Unokoti district, North Tripura. According to legend, Shiva was travelling with one crore gods and goddesses to visit Parvati's home (Kailash). He asked all his companions to wake up before sunrise to continue the journey. When morning came, none woke up and an angry Shiva cursed them all, turning them to stone — creating the famous stone images of Unakoti.
Bir Chandra Manikya — The Great Moderniser (1862–1896)

items: The site has enormous rock-cut and stone sculptures — the largest being a colossal 30-foot carving of Shiva's face known as 'Unakotiswara Kal Bhairav'
Other carvings include Ganesha, Nandi (bull), Durga, Vishnu, Kartik — all in rock-cut style
Dates: Approximately 7th–9th century CE (Gupta-Post Gupta period)
A natural stream flows through the site; the area is forested and scenic
UNESCO tentative World Heritage List: Unakoti has been proposed for UNESCO World Heritage Site status
Annual fair: Ashokastami Mela is held at Unakoti every year attracting thousands of pilgrims

blocks.content: 2.3 The Manikya Dynasty — Kingdom of Tripura (1280–1949 CE)

The Manikya dynasty ruled Tripura for approximately 669 years — one of the longest-ruling dynasties in South Asian history. The dynasty's origin is traced to the Twipra tribal chiefs who gradually adopted Hindu culture and became Rajputs, using the title 'Manikya' (meaning 'ruby gem'). The Manikya kings were devout Vaishnavites and Shakta worshippers who built numerous temples and patronised art, literature, and culture.

cells: First king to assume title 'Manikya'; consolidated the kingdom; considered the founder of the royal dynasty in its mature form
Expanded territory; defeated Sultan of Bengal multiple times; built Chaturdasha temple; patronised arts
Built temples; reformed administration; significant expansion of kingdom
Built the famous Ujjayanta Palace predecessor; composed poetry in Bengali
Philosopher-king; subject of the famous poem 'Rajmala' (chronicle of Tripura kings); known for justice
Built Ujjayanta-style structures; extended rule; relations with British
First to establish formal relations with British East India Company
Most important modern king; modernised Tripura; built roads, schools, hospitals; introduced printing press; composed poetry; transformed Agartala into a modern town
Continued modernisation; built Ujjayanta Palace (1901); helped Rabindranath Tagore get Jorasanko land
Supported British in WWI; Tripura's contribution to war effort
Last Maharaja of Tripura; signed Merger Agreement with India on 9 September 1949; Tripura merged with independent India

blocks.content: The Rajmala is the royal chronicle (vanshavali / itihas) of the Manikya kings of Tripura, written primarily in Bengali and Kokborok. It narrates the history of the Manikya dynasty from its origins to the 19th century. The Rajmala is a primary source for the history of Tripura and is comparable to the Rajatarangini of Kashmir. The chronicle was compiled under the orders of successive Manikya kings. It blends mythological origins with historical accounts of wars, alliances, and cultural patronage.

items: Original language: Kokborok (Tripuri language), later translated and expanded in Bengali
Contains genealogy of Manikya kings from semi-mythological origins
Describes wars with Bengal Sultanate, Mughal Nawabs, and neighbouring kingdoms
Cultural information about tribal traditions, festivals, and temple worship
The Rajmala is studied by historians as an authentic chronicle of northeast Indian medieval history

blocks.content: 2.5 Bir Chandra Manikya — The Great Moderniser (1862–1896)

items: The duration of the Manikya Dynasty spans from 1280 to 1949 CE.
Rajmala is the title of the ancient royal chronicle of the Tripura Kingdom.
Bir Chandra Manikya is tested frequently as 'The Great Moderniser' of Tripura.

blocks.content: Maharaja Bir Chandra Manikya is considered the greatest Manikya king and the architect of modern Tripura. His reforms transformed Tripura from a medieval kingdom to a progressive state that rivalled even British administered areas in certain respects.

items: Abolished slavery in Tripura — before British India passed similar laws
Established schools across Tripura; promoted women's education
Built roads connecting Agartala to different parts of the state
Introduced printing press (1870) — the first in the entire northeast India region
Established hospitals and dispensaries
Promoted Bengali language and literature; Agartala became a centre of Bengali literary renaissance in the late 19th century
His court attracted poets, scholars, and intellectuals including from Bengal
Composed poetry himself in Bengali and Kokborok

Relation with Rabindranath Tagore: Tagore visited Tripura multiple times; the Manikya royal family had a close relationship with Tagore; Tagore composed several works during his Tripura visits; 'Bisarjan' (play) is partly inspired by Tripura

blocks.content: NOTE: Maharaja Bir Chandra Manikya's introduction of the printing press in Tripura (1870) made Agartala the first city in northeast India to have a printing press — predating even Guwahati. This had a transformative effect on literacy, literature, and political consciousness in Tripura. His abolition of slavery also preceded similar measures in many British-administered territories.
